answer_summary: Wykoff emphasized patient and physician choice, timely access, and matching the right medicine to the patient. answer_summary: Wykoff said the wet AMD and GA pipeline should improve durability, improve absolute vision outcomes for some wet AMD patients, and produce better GA therapies. He highlighted gene therapy and self-administered subcutaneous approaches as investigational options that could reduce treatment burden, while noting they were not proven yet.

answer_summary: Wykoff said most US retina specialists use treat-and-extend or variants of it, usually moving through monthly drying, slow extension while treating every visit, and then maintenance just shorter than the recurrence interval. He noted some subretinal fluid may be tolerable, but emphasized continuous dosing and individualized maximum tolerated intervals.
answer_limitations: April 2020 article; answer reflects evidence and treatment options available at that time.

answer_summary: Wykoff said maximum tolerated interval is often fairly stable, citing TREX-AMD and VEGF suppression data, but a meaningful minority of patients can extend further if rechallenged. In practice, physicians may rechallenge every year or two depending on the patient and interval.
answer_limitations: Dated 2020 discussion; does not account for later longer-duration products.

answer_summary: Wykoff described variation in loading doses, tolerance of subretinal versus intraretinal fluid, home OCT interest, longest interval caps, and possible treatment cessation. His own approach is to treat monthly until the retina is as dry as possible, extend when appropriate, treat more frequently after recurrence at quarterly dosing, and recognize that many patients still need long-term consistent therapy.
answer_limitations: Broad answer covering several subtopics; practice patterns and home monitoring evidence have evolved since 2020.

answer_summary: Wykoff said active wet AMD may sometimes be observed or dosed infrequently when there is a disciform scar, very limited visual potential, and a well-sighted fellow eye. He also noted treatment may be stopped near end of life, and these decisions must be individualized.
answer_limitations: Short Q&A answer; does not provide a full decision algorithm.

answer_summary: Wykoff said missed injections are a real-world challenge because some eyes remain stable after one or two missed doses while others progress, and clinicians cannot reliably predict which pattern will occur. He noted that hospitalized patients often lack a good mechanism for routine outpatient ophthalmic care.
answer_limitations: Short 2020 answer; operational options may vary by facility and have changed since the COVID-era context.

answer_summary: Wykoff expected wet AMD innovation to focus on better durability and/or efficacy, including PDS with ranibizumab, longer-acting drugs such as faricimab, KSI-301, conbercept, and GB-102, and potentially disruptive gene therapy. He framed gene therapy as an ocular biofactory approach with promising early durability but still needing phase 2 learning.
answer_limitations: Historical April 2020 pipeline view; several named programs later changed status or evidence base.

answer_summary: Wykoff said retina surgeons should understand complement because GA was a major unmet need and the promising late-stage programs all targeted steps in the complement cascade. He cautioned that the pathway is more complex than anti-VEGF biology and that therapies are being developed despite incomplete mechanistic knowledge.
answer_limitations: GA-focused adjacent AMD interview, not nAMD-specific; January/February 2022 pipeline context predates approvals.

answer_summary: Wykoff highlighted avacincaptad targeting C5 and pegcetacoplan targeting C3 as the leading late-stage complement programs, with other programs targeting MAC, C1q, factor D, additional C3 inhibitors, and complement regulators. He emphasized these drugs appeared to slow GA growth rather than restore vision, with roughly 15% to 30% slowing in available data and potentially greater effects in extrafoveal lesions.
answer_limitations: GA-focused and dated before later approvals and label/safety experience; not a wet AMD treatment answer.

answer_summary: Wykoff said clinicians should know the expanding AMD options and proactively explain benefits and risks to patients, including PDS even if they are cautious about its safety profile. He viewed PDS as effective in appropriate patients when technique is meticulous, saw faricimab as noninferior with differentiated durability, and stressed maintaining current outcomes so patients can benefit from future therapies.
